findings.title: The isolation step 0.73.0 just added to the contract is defeated by a stale __pycache__, and the check it prescribes cannot see that: two same-size mutations of one file inside one second, and the second runs the first's bytecode
evidence: Measured this run, same procedure twice, one variable changed. With `__pycache__` left in place: mutant M3 (validate.py:429 `continue` becomes `break`) reported `1 passed in 0.01s` for tests/test_validate.py::test_the_state_validator_keeps_checking_after_a_malformed_entry, i.e. SURVIVED. With `__pycache__` swept and PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1: `1 failed in 0.05s`, i.e. KILLED. Killed 4 of 5 in the first pass, 5 of 5 in the second.

Mechanism, printed: after applying M2 (validate.py:198 `continue` becomes `break`) the source is 31075 bytes at mtime second 1788400567 and a .pyc is written; applying M3 gives an identical 31075 bytes at the identical mtime second 1788400567. CPython validates a cached .pyc on (source mtime seconds, source size), so M3's source loads M2's bytecode.

The prescribed check does not discriminate: in both runs `verdict_mcp.validate.__file__` printed the scratch path `.../scratchpad/tree/src/verdict_mcp/validate.py`. The path is right and the bytecode is wrong. `__cached__` was `.../tree/src/verdict_mcp/__pycache__/validate.cpython-313.pyc` in both.

Behavioural read-out, same probe: with the stale cache `validate()` returned ['findings[0] is not an object', "findings[1] (PRC-F-2) severity 'Huge' not in [...]"] and the guard test PASSES (mutant reported SURVIVED); after deleting `__pycache__` it returned only ['findings[0] is not an object'] and the guard test FAILS (mutant KILLED).

agents/verdict.md:221-227 (the paragraph 0.73.0 added) names PYTHONPATH and `print(<pkg>.__file__)` and says nothing about bytecode; docs/state-schema.md:319-326 repeats the same recipe for `verification.pythonpath`.

`cp -a <checkout> <scratch>` — the copy form the bash guard was widened in 0.65.0 to permit — carries every `__pycache__` in the tree, so the trap is armed by the contract's own recommended procedure.

root_cause.mechanism: CPython's cached-bytecode validation compares the source's mtime (truncated to whole seconds) and its size against the header of the .pyc. Successive injections into one file during a fast re-injection loop routinely land in the same second, and two mutations of the same kind — here `continue` to `break` at two different lines — produce files of identical size. When both hold, the interpreter reuses the previous injection's bytecode and the new injection is never executed.
root_cause.origin: Introduced as a contract gap by d21d4f9 (v0.73.0), which added the isolation paragraph and specified the import-path check as sufficient. The underlying interpreter behaviour is not a defect in this repository; the defect is that the procedure this repository mandates does not control for it and its stated verification cannot detect it.

class.pattern: searched for the same shape in the machine-side verifier: `_verify_findings`/`_run_test` in src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:399-534 sets PYTHONPATH but never sets PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE and never sweeps `__pycache__`. It creates one scratch checkout per run and then overwrites HEAD's test files into it once per finding (harness.py:508-517), so two findings whose cited test files differ but happen to have the same byte size, copied inside one second, would hit the same trap.

root_cause.trigger: A re-injection loop fast enough to write two mutations of one file inside the same clock second — which is every loop this contract asks for, since the whole point is that re-injection is cheap.
root_cause.latent_condition: The contract states one check (`__file__`) and treats it as sufficient for the whole claim "the copy runs its own code". A check that cannot fail for a whole class of the thing it certifies reads identically to one that can.
root_cause.fix_location: spec — agents/verdict.md §3 and the docs/state-schema.md twin. A machine-side belt-and-braces (PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE in the verifier's env) is a code change worth taking at the same time.

proof.evidence: Two runs of an identical re-injection over an identical scratch tree, differing only in whether `__pycache__` was swept: 4 of 5 mutants killed uncontrolled, 5 of 5 controlled. The one that flipped is M3, and the flip was reproduced a second time in isolation with the module's `__file__` and `__cached__` printed on both sides.

findings.title: The strict bash guard still permits archiving the checkout away — 0.71.0 closed the exact command the finding quoted, but `tar -cf <scratch>/loot.tar --remove-files <checkout>/hooks` is allowed, because every option token containing the letter `f` is treated as taking an argument and `--remove-files` swallows the operand
evidence: Seven-case probe against hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py at HEAD, VERDICT_STRICT=1, real git checkout as cwd: case B `tar -cf <scratch>/loot.tar --remove-files <repo>/hooks` returns rc=0 (ALLOW) where DENY is required; case C `tar -c -f <scratch>/loot.tar --remove-files <repo>/hooks` also rc=0.

The reported shape is closed: case A `tar --remove-files -cf <scratch>/loot.tar <repo>/src` returns rc=2 (DENY) at HEAD and rc=0 (ALLOW) at a6011ec — the same probe run against `git show a6011ec:hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py`, where all four deletion cases were allowed (4 mismatches) against 2 at HEAD.

Mechanism traced directly: `_check_tar(["-cf", "/s/loot.tar", "--remove-files", "/repo/hooks"], "/cwd")` yields `[]`; `_check_tar(["-c", "-f", "/s/loot.tar", "--remove-files", "/repo/hooks"], "/cwd")` yields `[]`.

hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:332-336 — `if t.startswith("-"): if "f" in t.lstrip("-"): next(it, None)`. `"--remove-files".lstrip("-")` is `"remove-files"`, which contains `f`, so the token after it is consumed as if it were an archive name.

The same bug misreads the tested order too: `_check_tar(["--remove-files", "-cf", "/s/x.tar", "/repo/src"], "/cwd")` yields the archive `/s/x.tar` as a removal target as well as `/repo/src`. The passing test is right for half the wrong reason — `--remove-files` swallowed `-cf`, not the archive name.

The gap is visible in this run's own coverage: facts.json per_file marks hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py lines 330-331 unexercised — the `if t in skip: next(it, None); continue` branch, which is exactly the split `-c -f` path case C walks. Production changed-line coverage fell 100% (run 9) to 94% (this run) on those two lines alone.

root_cause.mechanism: The new `--remove-files` operand loop parses tar options by substring rather than by an option table: any token starting with `-` whose remainder contains `f` is assumed to take a separate argument. `--remove-files` satisfies that test, so whatever follows it — including the checkout path it is about to delete — is skipped without being yielded as a candidate target.
root_cause.origin: ad05c6f (v0.71.0), the F-42 fix itself. The loop is new in that commit; `git diff a6011ec..HEAD -- hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` shows it added whole.

class.pattern: searched `hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` for the same substring-option shape: two sites, both in `_check_tar`. Line 334 is this finding. Line 310-311 uses the identical idiom for `x` and produces the mirror-image error (a false DENY on `--exclude`), filed separately as VERDICT-F-49. `grep -n 'lstrip("-")' hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` returns exactly those two lines; the other handlers (`_check_find`, `_check_awk`, the rsync/cp arms) test whole tokens against sets and are not affected.

root_cause.trigger: None needed — the hole never closed. What changed is that the fix made the quoted command deny, which reads as the finding being closed.
root_cause.latent_condition: The three tests added with the fix use only the token order the finding's title quoted (`--remove-files` first, `-cf` combined). No test varies the argument order, so the fix was verified against the sentence rather than against the behaviour. This is the same shape as the 0.70.0 fixture-freshness claim that VERDICT-F-47 corrected, one release later.
root_cause.fix_location: code — hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py `_check_tar`, which needs a real option table (`-f/--file` and `-C/--directory` take arguments; nothing else in tar's create path does) rather than a substring test.

proof.evidence: The same seven-case probe run against the previous commit's guard and against HEAD's: 4 deletion cases allowed at a6011ec, 2 still allowed at HEAD, controls (plain create allowed, extract-into-checkout denied, scratch-only deletion allowed) identical on both.

findings.title: The VERDICT_STRICT bash guard reads shell metacharacters inside quoted strings and heredoc bodies as live syntax and resolves phantom targets against the checkout, blocking read-only QA commands
evidence: Four blocked read-only commands this run, each costing a round trip. (1) A Python format spec `{rc:>3}` inside a single-quoted heredoc body: "output redirection targets '<checkout>/3} (a git checkout under /private/tmp)'".
(2) A string literal `"<tmp>"` inside the same kind of heredoc: "output redirection targets '<checkout>/\"))'".
(3) A `->` inside a module docstring: "output redirection targets '<checkout>/the'".

(4) NEW SHAPE, same family: `cd <scratchpad> && cat > trace2.py <<'EOF'` — a genuine redirect whose relative target was resolved against the tool's cwd rather than the `cd` in the same command, so a write to a temp scratch dir was refused as a write to the checkout: "output redirection targets '<checkout>/trace2.py'". Folded in here rather than given a new id because the harm and the file are the same; noted as a distinct mechanism.

Workaround used all four times: literal absolute paths and no `<`, `>` or `->` anywhere in a heredoc body. The guard's refusal of an unexpanded `$S/...` variable is by contrast a deliberate, well-messaged fail-closed and is not part of this finding.

findings.title: The same substring option parsing in the other direction: any tar flag containing the letter `x` reads as an extraction, so `tar --exclude=.venv -cf <scratch>/x.tar <checkout>/src` is denied as an overwrite of the current directory
evidence: `_check_tar(["--exclude=.venv", "-cf", "/s/x.tar", "/repo/src"], "/cwd")` yields `[('tar extract (overwrites in place)', '/cwd')]` — a create is reported as an extraction, and the flagged target is the cwd, which for a QA session is the checkout.
`_check_tar(["-cf", "/s/x.tar", "--exclude", "junk", "/repo/src"], "/cwd")` yields the same.
hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:310-311 — `extracting = (any(t.startswith("-") and "x" in t.lstrip("-") for t in args) ...)`. `"--exclude=.venv".lstrip("-")` contains `x`.
Archaeology: `git log -L 310,311:hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` names 27eabd5 (v0.45.0) as the commit that introduced this line. It predates the 0.71.0 tar work and was not touched by it.

Practical cost: `tar --exclude=.venv -cf <scratch>/backup.tar <checkout>` is the natural way to snapshot a checkout for a re-injection without dragging 49 MB of virtualenv along — the exact operation the contract's scratch-copy step asks for, refused.

root_cause.mechanism: Extraction is detected by testing whether the letter `x` appears anywhere in an option token's body, which is sound for bundled short flags (`-xzf`) and wrong for every long option containing an x. `--exclude`, `--xattrs` and `--extract`-adjacent spellings all match; the handler then reports an extract whose target defaults to the cwd.

class.pattern: the mirror of VERDICT-F-42's line 334. `grep -n 'lstrip("-")' hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py` returns exactly these two sites, and both should be replaced by the same option table.

root_cause.trigger: None; latent since v0.45.0 and only reachable by a `tar` invocation with a long option containing an x, which nothing in this repository's own tests uses.
root_cause.latent_condition: The tar handler has no test for a create with long options at all — the three tests added in 0.71.0 use short bundled flags exclusively.
root_cause.fix_location: code — hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:310-311, together with the F-42 fix at line 334.

proof.evidence: Direct invocation of the handler with and without the `--exclude` token: with it, an extract is reported against the cwd; without it, nothing is yielded and the identical create is allowed.

findings.title: The footnote 0.72.0 added to close VERDICT-F-45 reports the largest per-bucket count where its sentence scopes over every confirmation, so the published table says `Up to 17` of 28 confirmations are unrecorded when 21 of them are
evidence: Rendered from the committed .qa/state.json through `verdict_mcp.harness._render_calibration`, the published line reads: "*Up to 17 of those confirmations were settled before `outcome_basis` was recorded and are neither kind. They are counted in `held up` and in no other column…*"
The same state's per-bucket arithmetic: proven 24 confirmed − 0 measured − 7 claimed = 17; unstated 3 − 0 − 0 = 3; probable 1 − 0 − 0 = 1. Sum 21, maximum 17, total confirmed 28.

src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:1838-1839 — `unrecorded = max((v.get("confirmed", 0) - v.get("confirmed_measured", 0) - v.get("confirmed_claimed", 0) for v in buckets), default=0)`. The generator is per bucket; the sentence it feeds says "those confirmations", which is the whole `held up` column.

Reader consequence, which is precisely what VERDICT-F-45 was filed about: the table shows 28 held up and 0 measured, so subtracting the stated 17 leaves 11 that appear to be measured or the tester's word, when the true attributable count is 7 — all `claimed`, all in the proven row.

The fix is otherwise sound and fix-verified this run: re-injecting `if unrecorded:` as `if False:` fails tests/test_calibration.py::test_the_report_says_how_many_confirmations_predate_the_basis while the negative control test_no_such_line_when_every_confirmation_carries_a_basis still passes.

root_cause.mechanism: `max` over the buckets answers "what is the largest number of unrecorded confirmations in any one row"; the sentence asks "how many of the confirmations in this table are unrecorded". Those coincide only when a single bucket carries them all, which is true for by_proof_method (empty) and false for by_confidence here.

class.pattern: searched `src/verdict_mcp/harness.py` for other cross-bucket aggregates in the renderer: `grep -n 'max(\|sum(' src/verdict_mcp/harness.py` in `_render_calibration` returns only this one; the table rows themselves are rendered per bucket and are correct.

root_cause.trigger: Any project whose unrecorded confirmations span more than one confidence bucket — which this one's do, and have since the `outcome_basis` field was introduced.
root_cause.latent_condition: The test written with the fix asserts the line appears and does not assert its number against an independently computed total, so any aggregation function that returns a positive integer passes it.
root_cause.fix_location: code — sum the per-bucket differences, or print the count per row instead of one footnote for the table.

proof.evidence: The renderer's own output (`Up to 17`) against the same state's arithmetic (17 + 3 + 1 = 21 unrecorded of 28 confirmed), both computed in one pass over the committed state.json.

findings.title: Every finding's `first_seen` and `age_days` are stamped from the machine's local calendar while the run that stamps them is timestamped in UTC, so this run filed five findings dated 2026-09-02 inside a state whose own timestamp, report filename and INDEX row all read 2026-09-03
evidence: Found by the mandated pre-handoff self-check (contract §13) reading back the state this run had just written, and reproduced before filing.

src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:1214 `today = today or date.today()`. `date.today()` is the local calendar; every other clock in this module is UTC — harness.py:845 `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, harness.py:1657 and 1676 likewise, and `last_run.timestamp_utc` by name.
Measured on this machine at the moment of the run: `date.today()` returns 2026-09-02 while `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` returns 2026-09-03.

The artifacts disagree with each other as a result. In the first run-10 state written this session, `last_run.timestamp_utc` was 2026-09-03T01:44:59Z, the report was reports/2026-09-03-delta-run10.md and the INDEX row read 2026-09-03, while VERDICT-F-50 — filed for the first time by that same run — carried `first_seen: 2026-09-02`.

Ages inherit the error: VERDICT-F-21 has `first_seen: 2026-09-01` and was stamped `age_days: 1` when its true age at the run's own UTC timestamp is 2 days. §6 of the contract calls age the pressure and requires it to be shown, and the report prints this number.

harness.py:1246 makes the stamp permanent: `first_seen = (prior or {}).get("first_seen") or today.isoformat()`, and the value is copied into the permanent ledger, so a wrong date is carried for the life of the finding rather than recomputed.

root_cause.mechanism: `merge()` defaults its `today` argument to `date.today()`, which resolves against the host's timezone. For any run executed between 00:00 and 07:00 UTC on a US Pacific machine — that is, any evening run — the local calendar is one day behind the UTC calendar the rest of the run is measured in, so newly filed findings are dated to the previous day and every age is computed one day short.
root_cause.origin: Predates this range: `git diff a6011ec..HEAD -- src/verdict_mcp/harness.py` does not touch line 1214. It has been latent because every prior run of this project was made in local daytime, where the two calendars agree; run 10 at 01:44Z is the first to cross UTC midnight.

class.pattern: searched the module for other local-clock reads: `grep -n 'date.today()\|datetime.now(' src/verdict_mcp/harness.py` returns four sites — 845, 1657 and 1676 all pass `timezone.utc`, and 1214 is the only naive one. The INDEX row's own date was fixed to the state's UTC timestamp once already (VERDICT-F-24, and tests/test_artifact_check.py::test_an_index_row_dated_from_the_wrong_clock_is_named still guards it), which is why the INDEX and the findings now disagree: one half of the pair was corrected and the other was not.

root_cause.trigger: A run executed after UTC midnight but before local midnight. This is the first such run in the project's history, which is why nine previous runs did not surface it.
root_cause.latent_condition: The contract's own rule — §6, timestamps are measured, never remembered, via `date -u` — is enforced for the run timestamp and not for the derived dates the harness computes from it. Nothing checks that `first_seen` for a NEW finding equals the UTC date of the run that filed it.
root_cause.fix_location: code — pass the run's own UTC date into `merge()` (facts.json already carries `measured_at`), rather than letting it default to the host calendar. The check worth adding beside it is that a NEW finding's `first_seen` matches `last_run.timestamp_utc`'s date.

proof.evidence: The same instant read two ways on this host: `date.today()` gives 2026-09-02, `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` gives 2026-09-03, and the state written from it carries both values in different fields.

findings.title: The abandoned-run marker narrates any marker up to six hours old as "minutes ago", contradicting the age it records in the same object — this run's facts read `age_hours: 2.01` beside "minutes ago … Nothing is missing"
evidence: This run's .qa/facts.json: `"previous_attempt_this_run": {"started_utc": "2026-09-02T23:44:23Z", …, "age_hours": 2.01, "meaning": "an earlier attempt at this same commit, minutes ago — this run's own retry, not a lost run. Nothing is missing"}`.

src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:81 `RETRY_WINDOW_HOURS = 6` and harness.py:994 `age_h is not None and age_h <= RETRY_WINDOW_HOURS`, with the fixed string "minutes ago" at harness.py:999. Any marker from 0 to 6 hours old is described as minutes old.

The marker this run met was in fact two hours old and from a different session (the file is gitignored per-run scratch, `.qa/.gitignore:5`), so it was a crashed or superseded attempt rather than a retry of the run that read it. The chain conclusion happens to hold — nothing was finalized, so nothing is missing from runs.jsonl — but the harness reaches it from a description that is false.
Same shape as the footnote defects this project has already fixed twice (VERDICT-F-36, VERDICT-F-45): a rendered sentence asserting something the measured value beside it contradicts.

root_cause.mechanism: The narration string is written for the middle of the retry window rather than derived from the measured age, and the window is six hours wide.
root_cause.origin: The retry-window branch in `facts()`; unchanged by this range, so it predates a6011ec.

class.pattern: searched the harness for other hardcoded time words beside computed ages: `grep -n 'minutes ago\|hours ago\|just now' src/verdict_mcp/harness.py` returns only harness.py:999. The sibling `previous_run_incomplete` message states no age at all and is not affected.

root_cause.trigger: A marker older than a few minutes and younger than six hours — which is what a crashed overnight-adjacent run leaves.
root_cause.latent_condition: The retry branch collapses two different situations, 'my own retry' and 'someone else's crashed run at the same commit', into one sentence; the data cannot distinguish them, and the sentence claims the first.
root_cause.fix_location: code — derive the phrase from `age_h`, or drop the time word and let the recorded `age_hours` speak.

proof.evidence: The measured field and the narration are in the same JSON object in this run's facts.json, and the constant that governs the branch is 6 hours.

evidence: Re-injected in an isolated scratch copy: replacing `is_test_file`'s body with `return False` (src/verdict_mcp/harness.py:607-617) turns tests/test_diff_coverage.py::test_what_counts_as_a_test_file, ::test_the_production_percent_falls_when_production_coverage_falls and ::test_the_report_reads_production_first from `3 passed in 1.82s` into `2 failed, 1 passed in 1.40s`.

The split is honest, checked rather than trusted: recomputing by_kind from facts.json per_file gives production 32/34 (94%) and tests 101/119 (85%), matching the reported numbers, and 34 + 119 = 153 = the blended denominator with no double counting.

The classifier was audited over the whole repository, not the diff: of 74 tracked .py/.ts files exactly 35 classify as test (the 25 project tests, tests/conftest.py, 9 eval fixture test files and one .ts fixture test) and no production file is misclassified in either direction.

It earned its keep on its first live run: production changed-line coverage reads 94% against run 9's 100%, and the two unexercised lines it names (hooks/enforce_bash_scope.py:330-331) are exactly the branch carrying the live guard bypass reported as VERDICT-F-42. findings.title: Five non-equivalent operator and guard mutants in validate.py survive the whole 674-test suite — including the judgment validator's status-enum check and both of the PostToolUse hook's exit codes
evidence: All five re-applied by hand in an isolated scratch copy, each against the guard test written for it, with the instrument controlled first: unmutated, all five guards pass (`1 passed` each); mutated, all five fail (`1 failed` each). Killed 5 of 5.

The five: validate.py:214 `not in` becomes `in` (guard test_judgment_status_must_be_one_the_contract_knows); validate.py:198 `continue` becomes `break` (test_judgment_keeps_checking_after_a_malformed_entry); validate.py:429 `continue` becomes `break` (test_the_state_validator_keeps_checking_after_a_malformed_entry); validate.py:551 `return 2` becomes `return 0` (test_hook_mode_refuses_a_state_it_cannot_read); validate.py:556 `return 0` becomes `return 1` (test_hook_mode_is_silent_over_a_clean_state).

The scratch tree was restored byte-identically after every injection (`tree restored byte-identical: True`), and the module under test was confirmed to be the scratch's own (`verdict_mcp.validate.__file__` printed inside the scratch).

The first pass at this measurement read 4 of 5 — M3 SURVIVED — and that reading was wrong: it was running an earlier mutant's cached bytecode. Filed as VERDICT-F-50, and recorded in lessons.md, because the same error would have published a false survivor against a guard that works.
